result.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): B combines the vague 1-to-10 slider and the high default into its top issue and gives a concrete fix. It also proposes a preview of what the assistant would have done with the user's last five emails, and ties presets to the user not having seen the product work yet. A covers similar ground but runs eleven loosely weighted points and only offers an estimated summary of the settings' effect, not a preview on real mail. Neither answer names a specific element worth keeping beyond general praise. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers are well organized and catch the vague 1-to-10 slider and the risky default of 7. A is better on the rubric's core trust point: it suggests previewing what the assistant would have done with the user's last five emails before it acts, and it says plainly that the overload of choices comes before the product has shown any value. B only suggests a predicted summary of what Quill will do, and neither answer names a specific element worth keeping. Both run long with many near-equal items.
